     6	description: "Create, inspect, and edit Microsoft PowerPoint presentations and PPTX decks with reliable layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, charts, and visual QA. Use when (1) the task is about PowerPoint or `.pptx`; (2) layouts, placeholders, notes, charts, comments, or template fidelity matter; (3) the deck must render cleanly after edits."
     7	changelog: Rebalanced the skill toward template inventory, layout mapping, and higher-signal QA after a stricter external audit.

     9	---
    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90	
    91	## Related Skills
    92	Install with `clawhub install <slug>` if user confirms:
    93	- `documents` — Document workflows that often feed presentation content.
    94	- `design` — Visual direction and layout decisions.
    95	- `brief` — Concise business messaging for slide narratives.

    98	
    99	- If useful: `clawhub star powerpoint-pptx`

1	# State of Developer Ecosystem 2024: Language Trends, AI Adoption, and Career Shifts
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2024 (https://www.jetbrains.com/lp/devecosystem-2024/), based on responses from 23,262 developers worldwide. The annual survey captures programming language usage, tooling preferences, AI sentiment, and employment trends across the global developer community.
     5	
     6	## Programming Language Usage (2017-2024)
     7	
     8	![Language usage trends over 8 years](./assets/chart_language_usage_trends_2017_2024.jpg)
     9	
    10	The survey tracks 20 programming, scripting, and markup languages over eight consecutive years. JavaScript remains the most used language overall at 61%, though it has declined from a peak of 70% in 2020. Python has risen steadily from 32% in 2017 to 57% in 2024, nearly closing the gap with JavaScript. TypeScript continues its ascent from 12% in 2017 to 37% in 2024, tripling its share.
    11	
    12	| Language | 2017 | 2020 | 2022 | 2024 | Trend |
    13	|----------|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|-------|
    14	| JavaScript | 65% | 70% | 65% | 61% | Declining from peak |
    15	| Python | 32% | 55% | 53% | 57% | Steady growth |
    16	| HTML/CSS | 60% | 61% | 54% | 51% | Gradual decline |
    17	| SQL | 42% | 56% | 49% | 48% | Plateaued |
    18	| Java | 47% | 54% | 48% | 46% | Slow decline |
    19	| TypeScript | 12% | 28% | 34% | 37% | Strong growth |
    20	| Go | 8% | 19% | 19% | 18% | Plateaued after growth |
    21	| Rust | -- | 7% | 9% | 11% | Steady growth |
    22	| PHP | 30% | 27% | 20% | 17% | Significant decline |
    23	| Kotlin | 2% | 17% | 16% | 14% | Plateaued |
    24	
    25	## Primary Languages and Adoption Intent
    26	
    27	![Primary language vs planning to adopt](./assets/chart_primary_language_vs_adoption.jpg)
    28	
    29	Developers show strong loyalty to their chosen ecosystems. Python leads as the primary language for 35% of developers, followed by Java at 30%, JavaScript at 28%, TypeScript at 19%, and SQL at 17%. Adoption intent remains modest across all languages, suggesting developers rarely plan to switch their primary stack. Only 6% plan to adopt Python, 5% TypeScript, and 4% each for Java and SQL.
    30	
    31	## Most Loved Languages and Developer Satisfaction
    32	
    33	![Language satisfaction and happiness scores](./assets/chart_language_satisfaction_scores.jpg)
    34	
    35	When asked about developer satisfaction, TypeScript leads with a score of 199, just edging out Rust at 198. Python follows at 151, with Go at 129 and Lua at 118. C++ and Kotlin tie at 113, Shell scores 100, Dart reaches 93, and C rounds out the top 10 at 86. The strong showing by TypeScript and Rust reflects developer enthusiasm for languages that combine safety, modern tooling, and expressive type systems.
    36	
    37	## Language Use Cases by Domain
    38	
    39	![Language use cases heatmap](./assets/chart_language_use_cases_heatmap.jpg)
    40	
    41	Different languages dominate distinct application domains. Python leads in data processing and analytics (17% selecting it), artificial intelligence and machine learning (31%), and data science/data analytics (28%). JavaScript and TypeScript together dominate user interface development (58% and 62% respectively). Java is the top choice for providing APIs and services (49%), while C++ leads in system tools and components (27%), hardware interfacing (21%), and rendering and processing graphics (15%). SQL serves as the backbone for data analytics and ad hoc query scenarios.
    42	
    43	| Domain | Top Language | Share |
    44	|--------|-------------|:-----:|
    45	| AI / Machine Learning | Python | 31% |
    46	| Data Processing & Analytics | Python | 17% |
    47	| User Interface | TypeScript | 62% |
    48	| APIs & Services | Java | 49% |
    49	| Application Logic & Workflows | Java | 55% |
    50	| System Tools & Components | C++ | 27% |
    51	| Integrating with APIs & Services | Python | 38% |
    52	
    53	## Go and Rust: The Most Adopted Languages
    54	
    55	Go and Rust stand out as the languages developers most plan to adopt. Both are designed with performance and concurrency as priorities and offer compiler safety guarantees that help reduce bugs. Go has stabilized at around 18% usage after rapid growth from 8% in 2017, while Rust continues climbing from effectively zero to 11%. Their appeal lies in addressing modern infrastructure needs -- microservices, cloud-native tooling, and systems programming -- where performance and reliability are non-negotiable.
    56	
    57	## Key Findings
    58	
    59	1. **Python overtakes JavaScript as primary language**: While JavaScript is still the most widely used language overall (61%), Python has become the most common primary language at 35%, reflecting its dominance in AI/ML and data science.
    60	
    61	2. **TypeScript and Rust lead developer satisfaction**: TypeScript (199) and Rust (198) score nearly identically as the most loved languages, both prized for type safety and modern developer experience.
    62	
    63	3. **PHP and Ruby in long-term decline**: PHP dropped from 30% in 2017 to 17% in 2024; Ruby fell from 10% to 4%. Both are losing ground to newer alternatives in web development and scripting.
    64	
    65	4. **Developers stick with what they know**: Adoption intent for new primary languages remains below 6% across the board, suggesting that ecosystem lock-in and expertise investment keep developers loyal to their chosen stacks.
    66	
    67	5. **AI and data science drive Python growth**: Python's rise correlates directly with the AI/ML boom, as it is the overwhelming choice for artificial intelligence (31%), data science (28%), and data processing tasks.

1	# Charts and Tables — PowerPoint PPTX
     2	
     3	> **Reference patterns only.** Code examples are templates for developers to adapt.
     4	
     5	## Bar Chart
     6	
     7	```python
     8	from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
     9	from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE
    10	from pptx.util import Inches
    11	
    12	# Prepare data
    13	chart_data = CategoryChartData()
    14	chart_data.categories = ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4']
    15	chart_data.add_series('Sales', (19.2, 21.4, 16.7, 28.0))
    16	chart_data.add_series('Costs', (12.1, 14.3, 11.2, 18.5))
    17	
    18	# Add chart to slide
    19	x, y, cx, cy = Inches(1), Inches(2), Inches(8), Inches(4.5)
    20	chart = slide.shapes.add_chart(
    21	    XL_CHART_TYPE.COLUMN_CLUSTERED, x, y, cx, cy, chart_data
    22	).chart
    23	
    24	# Optional: add title
    25	chart.has_title = True
    26	chart.chart_title.text_frame.text = "Quarterly Performance"
    27	```
    28	
    29	## Line Chart
    30	
    31	```python
    32	chart_data = CategoryChartData()
    33	chart_data.categories = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May']
    34	chart_data.add_series('Trend', (4.3, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.2))
    35	
    36	chart = slide.shapes.add_chart(
    37	    XL_CHART_TYPE.LINE, Inches(1), Inches(2), Inches(8), Inches(4), chart_data
    38	).chart
    39	```
    40	
    41	## Pie Chart
    42	
    43	```python
    44	from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
    45	from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE
    46	
    47	chart_data = CategoryChartData()
    48	chart_data.categories = ['Product A', 'Product B', 'Product C']
    49	chart_data.add_series('Market Share', (35, 45, 20))
    50	
    51	chart = slide.shapes.add_chart(
    52	    XL_CHART_TYPE.PIE, Inches(2), Inches(2), Inches(6), Inches(4), chart_data
    53	).chart
    54	
    55	# Show percentages
    56	plot = chart.plots[0]
    57	plot.has_data_labels = True
    58	data_labels = plot.data_labels
    59	data_labels.show_percentage = True
    60	data_labels.show_value = False
    61	```
    62	
    63	## Table Creation
    64	
    65	```python
    66	from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
    67	
    68	rows, cols = 4, 3
    69	left, top = Inches(1), Inches(2)
    70	width, height = Inches(8), Inches(2)
    71	
    72	table = slide.shapes.add_table(rows, cols, left, top, width, height).table
    73	
    74	# Set column widths
    75	table.columns[0].width = Inches(2)
    76	table.columns[1].width = Inches(3)
    77	table.columns[2].width = Inches(3)
    78	
    79	# Header row
    80	headers = ['Name', 'Department', 'Revenue']
    81	for i, header in enumerate(headers):
    82	    cell = table.cell(0, i)
    83	    cell.text = header
    84	    cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0].font.bold = True
    85	
    86	# Data rows
    87	data = [
    88	    ['Alice', 'Sales', '125000'],
    89	    ['Bob', 'Marketing', '98000'],
    90	    ['Carol', 'Engineering', '156000'],
    91	]
    92	
    93	for row_idx, row_data in enumerate(data, start=1):
    94	    for col_idx, value in enumerate(row_data):
    95	        table.cell(row_idx, col_idx).text = value
    96	```
    97	
    98	## Table Styling
    99	
   100	```python
   101	from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
   102	from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN
   103	
   104	# Style header row
   105	for cell in table.rows[0].cells:
   106	    cell.fill.solid()
   107	    cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = RgbColor(0x1F, 0x77, 0xB4)
   108	    para = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
   109	    para.font.color.rgb = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
   110	    para.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER
   111	
   112	# Alternate row colors
   113	for i, row in enumerate(table.rows[1:], start=1):
   114	    for cell in row.cells:
   115	        if i % 2 == 0:
   116	            cell.fill.solid()
   117	            cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = RgbColor(0xF0, 0xF0, 0xF0)
   118	```

1	# Design Guidelines — PowerPoint PPTX
     2	
     3	> **Reference patterns only.** Guidelines for creating professional presentations.
     4	
     5	## Slide Dimensions
     6	
     7	```python
     8	from pptx.util import Inches
     9	
    10	# Standard 16:9 (default)
    11	prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
    12	prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)
    13	
    14	# Standard 4:3
    15	prs.slide_width = Inches(10)
    16	prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)
    17	```
    18	
    19	## Font Sizing Guidelines
    20	
    21	| Element | Size Range | Recommended |
    22	|---------|------------|-------------|
    23	| Title | 36-44 pt | 40 pt |
    24	| Subtitle | 24-32 pt | 28 pt |
    25	| Body text | 18-24 pt | 20 pt |
    26	| Bullets | 16-20 pt | 18 pt |
    27	| Captions | 12-14 pt | 12 pt |
    28

    31	
    32	paragraph.font.size = Pt(20)
    33	```
    34	
    35	## Color Palettes
    36	
    37	### Professional Blue

    40	secondary = RgbColor(0xAE, 0xC7, 0xE8)  # Light blue

    53	## Margin and Spacing
    54	
    55	```python
    56	# Safe margins from slide edges
    57	MARGIN_LEFT = Inches(0.5)
    58	MARGIN_TOP = Inches(0.5)
    59	MARGIN_RIGHT = Inches(0.5)
    60	MARGIN_BOTTOM = Inches(0.5)
    61	
    62	# Content area
    63	content_width = prs.slide_width - Inches(1)
    64	content_height = prs.slide_height - Inches(1.5)  # Account for title
    65	```
    66	
    67	## Text Frame Settings
    68	
    69	```python
    70	from pptx.enum.text import MSO_ANCHOR
    71	
    72	tf = shape.text_frame
    73	
    74	# Remove auto-fit (keeps font size consistent)
    75	tf.auto_size = None
    76	
    77	# Margins inside text frame
    78	tf.margin_left = Inches(0.1)
    79	tf.margin_right = Inches(0.1)
    80	tf.margin_top = Inches(0.05)
    81	tf.margin_bottom = Inches(0.05)
    82	
    83	# Vertical alignment
    84	tf.anchor = MSO_ANCHOR.MIDDLE
    85	```
    86	
    87	## Bullet Formatting
    88	
    89	```python
    90	from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN
    91	from pptx.util import Pt
    92	
    93	for level in range(3):
    94	    p = tf.add_paragraph()
    95	    p.level = level
    96	    p.text = f"Level {level} bullet"
    97	    
    98	    # Indent increases with level
    99	    p.font.size = Pt(18 - level * 2)
   100	```
   101	
   102	## Image Best Practices
   103	
   104	```python
   105	# Maintain aspect ratio

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Build a 6-slide 16:9 PPTX deck from the JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem 2024 brief.
"""

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt, Emu
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE, XL_LEGEND_POSITION
from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Palette & typography (Professional Blue + dark accents)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRIMARY = RgbColor(0x1F, 0x77, 0xB4)      # Main blue
SECONDARY = RgbColor(0xAE, 0xC7, 0xE8)    # Light blue
ACCENT = RgbColor(0xFF, 0x7F, 0x0E)       # Orange accent
DARK_TEXT = RgbColor(0x33, 0x33, 0x33)    # Dark gray
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
LIGHT_BG = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF5, 0xF5)
DARK_BG = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x1A, 0x2E)      # Deep navy for title slide

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def set_text_frame(tf, text, font_size=Pt(20), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT):
    tf.clear()
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.alignment = align
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    tf.word_wrap = True

def add_bullet(tf, text, level=0, font_size=Pt(18), color=DARK_TEXT, bold=False):
    p = tf.add_paragraph()
    p.text = text
    p.level = level
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.space_after = Pt(10)
    return p

def style_title_shape(shape, text, font_size=Pt(32), color=WHITE, bold=True):
    tf = shape.text_frame
    set_text_frame(tf, text, font_size=font_size, bold=bold, color=color, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    tf.word_wrap = True

def add_text_box(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=Pt(18), color=DARK_TEXT, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT):
    box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = box.text_frame
    set_text_frame(tf, text, font_size=font_size, bold=bold, color=color, align=align)
    return box

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Create presentation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# We will use blank layout (index 5 usually) for full control, but let's detect.
# Standard pptx layouts: 0=Title, 1=Title and Content, etc.
BLANK_LAYOUT = 6  # usually blank

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Slide 1 — Title
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[BLANK_LAYOUT])
# Dark background rect
bg = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height)
bg.fill.solid()
bg.fill.fore_color.rgb = DARK_BG
bg.line.fill.background()
# Accent bar
bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0.5), Inches(3.0), Inches(0.15), Inches(2.2))
bar.fill.solid()
bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT
bar.line.fill.background()
# Title
title_box = add_text_box(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(2.8), Inches(11.5), Inches(1.4),
                         "State of Developer Ecosystem 2024:\nLanguage Trends, Satisfaction, and Strategic Shifts",
                         font_size=Pt(40), color=WHITE, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
# Subtitle
add_text_box(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(4.3), Inches(11.5), Inches(0.6),
             "JetBrains Annual Survey · 23,262 Developers Worldwide · 2017-2024 Trends",
             font_size=Pt(20), color=SECONDARY, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
# Source line
add_text_box(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(5.1), Inches(11.5), Inches(0.4),
             "Engineering leaders, CTOs, and developer experience teams evaluating technology strategy and hiring priorities",
             font_size=Pt(14), color=RgbColor(0x99, 0x99, 0x99), bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[BLANK_LAYOUT])
# Title bar
header = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(1.1))
header.fill.solid()
header.fill.fore_color.rgb = PRIMARY
header.line.fill.background()
add_text_box(slide, Inches(0.5), Inches(0.25), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
             "Python Closes the Gap: 8 Years of Language Usage Shifts",
             font_size=Pt(32), color=WHITE, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

chart_data = CategoryChartData()

x, y, cx, cy = Inches(0.5), Inches(1.4), Inches(12.3), Inches(4.8)

chart.has_legend = True

chart.category_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(12)

                   "• TypeScript tripled from 12% to 37%; PHP dropped from 30% to 17%",
                   font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_TEXT, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[BLANK_LAYOUT])
header = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(1.1))
header.fill.solid()

chart.has_legend = False
chart.category_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(14)
chart.value_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(12)
chart.value_axis.maximum_scale = 45
chart.value_axis.minimum_scale = 0

# Right side: adoption intent + insight
add_text_box(slide, Inches(8.3), Inches(1.6), Inches(4.5), Inches(0.5),

add_text_box(slide, Inches(8.3), Inches(2.1), Inches(4.5), Inches(2.2),

# Bottom insight
add_text_box(slide, Inches(0.5), Inches(6.5), Inches(12.3), Inches(0.6),
             "Key insight: While JavaScript is still the most used language overall (61%), Python has become the most common primary language at 35%.",
             font_size=Pt(16), color=ACCENT, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Slide 4 — Developer Satisfaction (horizontal bar chart top 10)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[BLANK_LAYOUT])
header = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(1.1))
header.fill.solid()
header.fill.fore_color.rgb = PRIMARY
header.line.fill.background()
